title: A First Look at PISA 2025
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman offers a first pass through the 2025 PISA results, arguing England's traditionalist, Michael Gove-era reforms have held steady while progressive-reform Scotland and Wales continued declining in reading and mathematics against a backdrop of overall OECD decline from 2015 to 2025, making England one of the few systems bucking the broader trend. He treats Finland's long-mythologized progressive model as decisively settled by the data, noting England now outperforms Finland on all three PISA measures, and warns against treating Estonia as the next model system given emerging signs of reading decline there too. His most pointed methodological move is directly testing a specific claim made by education commentator Adam Voigt, that Japan's 2021 shift toward active learning explained its rise to third in reading by 2022, by checking whether that improvement held up in the newly released 2025 data; it did not, with Japan declining on all three measures since 2022, leading Ashman to suggest the active-learning explanation was likely a temporary correlation rather than a causal driver. He notes Australia's own mathematics trajectory as a specific, serious concern he attributes to curriculum quality, while crediting both Australia and the UK for scoring above the OECD average on inclusion and socioeconomic fairness. The piece closes with an explicit methodological caution against over-relying on cross-country rankings, since the pool of participating countries changes between rounds, arguing direction-of-travel and position changes over time are more informative than static rank comparisons.
points: Uses newly released 2025 PISA data to directly test and falsify a specific causal claim made only a few years earlier (that Japan's 2021 active-learning curriculum reform explained its 2022 reading rise), modeling how to treat an attractive causal story as a testable prediction rather than settled fact.

Treats Finland's reading and mathematics scores as empirically decisive on a long-running policy debate, noting England now outperforms Finland on all three PISA measures, directly undercutting the years-long 'Finland has no standardized testing and it works' narrative.

Explicitly warns against 'educational tourism' toward Estonia as the next Finland-replacement model, citing emerging signs of reading decline there as a caution against premature international policy borrowing.
Names curriculum quality specifically, not funding, teacher training, or demographics, as his working explanation for Australia's worrying mathematics trajectory.

States an explicit methodological caveat against over-interpreting cross-country rankings, since the number of participating countries changes between PISA rounds, arguing direction-of-travel comparisons are more defensible than static rank comparisons even though causal claims still cannot be made definitively.
quotes: England's results have broadly held since the last round of PISA in 2022. In contrast, Scotland and Wales have continued their declines in reading and mathematics, with science being the one bright spot.
The OECD average score in all three areas has declined from 2015 to 2025 and so it is England that is bucking this trend.

Can we please put this to bed now? Nobody should bang on any more about how teachers in Finland have masters degrees and there's no standardised testing. England now outperforms Finland on all three measures.
Educational tourists should leave Estonia well alone because when countries start listening to such tourists, they tend to make poor choices.

Japan's improvement in reading coincides directly with a deliberate move away from passive reception and toward active intellectual engagement. At the time, I was sceptical that a change to curriculum in 2021 would have had any discernible effect on 2022 PISA results. The 2025 results now demonstrate that Japan has declined on all three measures since 2022.
Australia's mathematics trajectory is deeply worrying and it probably reflects the poverty of our mathematics curriculum.

Politicians like to talk about rankings, but these don't even make sense on their own terms because the number of participating countries keeps changing. Instead, I think it is most useful to look at the direction of travel
